newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe privatisation seen as key to economy.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe privatisation seen as key to economy.

text.p: Zimbabwe's farm-based economy is expected to grow by up to seven percent in 1997 and economists say it could expand even more if a protracted privatisation programme finally comes on stream.
"That's (privatisation) the primary issue to watch in the coming year," said John Robertson, one of the southern African state's leading private economic consultants.
"If it does really happen...and the government takes its housekeeping responsibilities more seriously, then the economy is finally taking off on a long, happy flight," he told Reuters.

Gross domestic product (GDP) rose by an estimated five percent in 1996 on the back of a good agricultural season. But economists say growth could have been higher if the government of President Robert Mugabe had privatised loss-making state firms bleeding the economy.
Mugabe has dithered over privatisation since 1991 when he ditched a 10-year disastrous experiment with socialism, which many say ploughed the economy into the ground.
Plans to privatise dozens of state enterprises, ranging from a cotton marketing agency to one of Africa's largest steel producers, have mostly come to nothing.
The government says it is still drawing up "a proper plan" to ensure the programme runs in tandem with a long-standing promise to economically empower Zimbabwe's majority black population.

But some critics suspect Mugabe -- Zimbabwe's sole ruler since independence from Britain in 1980 -- is a reluctant backer of the scheme because he uses state companies to exercise political patronage.
In a year-end address to parliament two weeks ago, Mugabe pledged again that he would expedite the process, and although he gave no details some people believe 1997 may see progress.

"I think the privatisation programme will move a bit faster next year (1997) because I think (the ruling party) ZANU-PF has found a way of making sure its supporters benefit from the process," said political analyst John Makumbe of Harare's University of Zimbabwe.

Four months ago, the government ignored unprecedented public criticism to award a Malaysian power company YTL Corp Bhd a deal to privatise Zimbabwe's Hwange thermal power station without going through a tender or fulfilling its commitment of giving black investors a stake.

Few blacks have any significant capital, and Makumbe and Charles Rukuni, editor of a political and economic newsletter, The Insider, say Mugabe may direct state-owned or dominated financial houses to give loans to some blacks to help them acquire shares under the privatisation programme.
In the long-term, the government has set up a National Investment Trust where it plans to warehouse some shares for blacks from the privatised firms.

Local analysts say there is also mounting economic pressure, including a perennial battle against a high budget deficit, which if forcing the Zimbabwean government to privatise. Government expenditure eats about 40 percent of GDP.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank say they are unlikely to provide financial support to Zimbabwe's new five-year economic reform programme until the government shows progress in cutting state spending.
Other key Western donors, who were marshalled by the IMF and the bank to back Zimbabwe's last five-year reform programme, say they will take their lead from the two organisations.
